sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content: Global equities suffered a brutal, AI-led sell-off that spread across every region. MSCI World fell roughly **7%** (approx., verify before merging), with MSCI Developed Markets broadly similar (approx., verify before merging) and MSCI Emerging Markets more resilient, down low single digits (approx., verify before merging). In the US the S&P 500 slumped **8.6%** to about **6,910** — its worst week since April 2025 and into correction — the Nasdaq Composite dropped **10.0%** to **22,617.73** and the Dow fell **8.0%** to **48,147.33**. The mega-cap MAG7 cohort was crushed as Nvidia tumbled about **23%** on the week. Europe's Euro Stoxx 50 ended near **5,942**, down roughly **6%** (approx., verify before merging), as the STOXX 600 lost **5.80%**. sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
US equities endured their worst week since April 2025 as the AI trade unwound violently. The S&P 500 slumped **8.6%** to about **6,910**, closing more than **10%** below its 6 October record of **7,818.93** and entering correction territory. The Nasdaq Composite tumbled **10.0%** to **22,617.73** and the Dow fell **8.0%** to **48,147.33**.

Mega-cap technology led the rout. Nvidia lost roughly **23%** over the week — including a **14%** plunge on Friday — as investors questioned stretched AI valuations and the durability of hyperscaler capex, dragging the broader MAG7 cohort sharply lower and leaving semiconductors as the week's clear laggards.

Macro signals were mixed. The University of Michigan's one-year inflation expectations eased to **3.7%** from October's **4.7%**, but the NAHB housing index slid to a 14-year low of **25**. With inflation still sticky, investors continued to price a December Fed hike, keeping sentiment fragile into the weekend.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equities were swept up in the global risk-off wave, with the pan-European STOXX 600 falling **5.80%** — its steepest weekly drop since March — and the UK's FTSE 100 down **5.10%**. The Euro Stoxx 50 shed **2.81%** on Friday alone to close near **5,942**.

The sell-off was broad rather than domestic. Every major European index ended the week lower as an AI-driven pivot out of risk assets rippled across equities, with technology- and semiconductor-exposed names such as the chip-equipment makers bearing the brunt of the declines.

Rate dynamics offered little cushion. Although regional inflation data stayed relatively contained, hawkish Fed expectations and a firmer dollar weighed on sentiment, leaving cyclical and growth-oriented sectors leading the losses while more defensive pockets held up comparatively better.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Asian markets bore the sharpest losses as the AI chip trade unravelled. Japan's Nikkei 225 sank **7.7%** to around **56,437**, with the TOPIX off **6.78%**, while Taiwan's market plunged **6.2%** — its worst week since 1991 — and South Korea's KOSPI fell **5.2%**.

China proved a relative haven. The CSI 300 slipped just **0.76%** to **3,954.57** and Hong Kong's Hang Seng eased **1.89%** on Friday to **22,410.80**, cushioned by domestic policy support and lighter AI exposure than its regional peers.

The semiconductor cycle dominated flows. Heavy selling in chip and AI-linked exporters, combined with a stronger dollar and rising US rate expectations, pressured North Asian technology supply chains and sapped regional risk appetite across the board.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The US dollar extended its dominance, with the DXY climbing to a fresh 18-month high in a fourth straight weekly gain, up about **0.4%**, as risk-off flows and hawkish Fed pricing widened rate differentials. Convera framed the move as safe-haven demand overwhelming fading AI optimism.

The majors buckled. EUR/USD fell about **0.5%** to break below **1.10** — down nearly **2%** on the month — with buyers emerging near **1.0950**, while sterling slid to a one-year low as contrasting BoE repricing and global drivers pulled the pound in different directions.

The yen stayed under pressure, with USD/JPY near its highest since early September as widening Fed rate expectations drove the differential. Broad dollar strength and heightened risk aversion kept most emerging-market currencies on the back foot through the week.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
Commodities extended a punishing run. Saxo noted the Bloomberg Commodity index heading for a fifth straight weekly decline, down around **13%** from its peak, as rising yields, a stronger dollar and year-end positioning weighed on the complex.

Precious and industrial metals led the rout. Gold tumbled more than **7%** — its worst week since March — to near **$3,590** an ounce, its lowest since September 2025, while silver slumped about **13%**, as a hawkish Fed and AI-driven liquidation hit crowded longs across platinum and copper too.

Energy diverged. Crude retreated from its September highs as a lull in US-Iran tensions eased Strait of Hormuz supply fears, though demand worries tied to the AI-trade unwind added to the downward pressure, leaving the cross-asset message firmly risk-off.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
Government bonds rallied as the equity rout triggered a flight to safety. The 10-year UST yield fell back below **5%** to around **4.9%** — a fifth consecutive daily decline — while the 2-year dropped roughly **12bp** to about **4.7%**, its steepest weekly fall since August 2025.

The curve steepened modestly as front-end yields fell faster than the long end, with safe-haven demand overwhelming sticky-inflation concerns. Even so, Edward Jones noted investors still expected the Fed to hike in December, and possibly again in January, as it keeps focus on bringing inflation back to target.

Credit tone softened with the risk-off mood. While high-grade bonds benefited from the duration rally, the sharp equity decline and AI-valuation fears pressured riskier HY spreads, keeping overall credit sentiment cautious into the weekend.
